---
title: "Same data, two answers"
---

How much do house prices rise when incomes rise? Take the 48 contiguous US
states and the District of Columbia, 1975 to 2003, and regress log house prices
on log income in each state. The average of the 49 slopes is 0.30: a 10% rise
in income goes with a 3% rise in prices. Now allow for one more thing. Every
state feels the same national forces, interest rates and credit conditions,
each to its own degree. With that allowed for, the elasticity is 1.14. Same
data, almost four times the answer [@holly2010; @croissant2019, pp. 197–199].
This Part is about why.

A **panel** follows the same units, here states, over several periods. Its
promise is that each state is compared with itself over time, so everything
fixed about a state drops out. Its catch is that the states are not
independent of each other. A national shock moves them all at once, and in
the picture below it is hard to see 49 separate stories:

```{r}
#| label: s0-0-together
#| fig-cap: "Log house prices (left) and their annual growth (right) in 49
#|   US states, 1975–2003. Grey: one line per state. Black: the cross-state
#|   average. Prices are an index with 1980 = 100 in every state, which is
#|   why the lines pinch together in 1980."
#| fig-alt: "Two line charts with 49 thin grey lines and one thick black
#|   line each. On the left, log price indices rise and fall in waves that
#|   most states share, around the average. On the right, annual growth
#|   rates swing together: booms and busts hit most states in the same
#|   years, by different amounts."
data("HousePricesUS", package = "pder")
lp <- with(HousePricesUS, tapply(log(price), list(year, names), identity))
growth <- diff(lp)
op <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
graphics::matplot(as.numeric(rownames(lp)), lp, type = "l", lty = 1,
                  col = "grey75", xlab = "year", ylab = "log price index",
                  main = "Levels")
graphics::lines(as.numeric(rownames(lp)), rowMeans(lp), lwd = 3)
graphics::matplot(as.numeric(rownames(growth)), growth, type = "l", lty = 1,
                  col = "grey75", xlab = "year", ylab = "annual growth",
                  main = "Growth rates")
graphics::lines(as.numeric(rownames(growth)), rowMeans(growth), lwd = 3)
graphics::par(op)
```

In equations, state *i* in year *t* follows

$$
y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta x_{it} + u_{it}, \qquad
u_{it} = \lambda_i f_t + \varepsilon_{it}.
$$

Here $\alpha_i$ is everything fixed about the state, $f_t$ is the national
shock in year *t*, and $\lambda_i$ is how strongly state *i* feels it. Fixed
effects remove $\alpha_i$. Year effects remove $f_t$, but only if every state
feels it equally, $\lambda_i = 1$. When the loadings differ and the shock also
moves income, the shock leaks into $\hat\beta$. That leak is the gap between
0.30 and 1.14.

**In this Part.**

1. **Panel shape.** How many units, how many years, and whether every unit is
   observed every year decide which tools work
   ([panel shape](panel-spat.qmd#sec-panel-shape)).
2. **Common shocks.** Do the units move together more than chance allows,
   and how strongly? The CD test answers the first question
   ([CD tests](panel-spat.qmd#sec-csd-tests)); the exponent α, which counts
   how many units a shock reaches, answers the second
   ([α](panel-spat.qmd#sec-csd-exponent)).
3. **Removing common shocks.** Add the cross-state averages of prices and
   income to each state's regression, so they stand in for $f_t$. This is
   common correlated effects, CCE, and it gives the 1.14
   ([CCE](panel-spat.qmd#sec-cce)).
4. **Unit roots.** Do prices drift with no level to return to? If so, a
   regression of one drifting series on another can find a link that is not
   there ([unit roots](unit-roots.qmd)).
5. **Still to come.** Long-run relations between drifting series, the
   structure of the errors, static and dynamic panel estimators, and spatial
   spillovers between neighbours.
